newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel delays vote on capital market reform.
newsitem.headline: Israel delays vote on capital market reform.

text.p: A panel set up to discuss a proposed tax on short- and medium-term savings will delay presenting its recommendations to the cabinet which was due for a vote on Friday, a Treasury spokesman said.
The Treasury had said the recommendations, originally set to be handed over to the government last Sunday, could be submitted on November 1.
The spokesman did not give a reason for the delay and no fresh date has been scheduled for the presentation.

The panel, which is seeking a compromise to the Treasury's proposal to tax interest paid on savings of up to 10 years, was formed following a marathon cabinet meeting nearly three weeks ago on capital market reform.
The committee is made up of Treasury Director General David Brodett, Bank of Israel director David Klein and deputy director general of the prime minister's office Moshe Lion.

The savings tax is a crucial part of a package on capital market reform proposed by the Treasury. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who took office in June promising not to raise taxes, led the cabinet in its decision to postpone a vote.

The Treasury is now proposing a tax of 3.5 percent on nominal interest paid on savings instead of the five percent originally proposed. Also, the tax would be levied only on savings of up to five years instead of 10.
While the Bank of Israel has come out in favour of the compromise, the prime minister's office is still said to be opposed to any tax.
The Treasury has argued that a tax on savings is needed to offset other parts of the reform package, such as lowering taxes on long-term savings and on dividends.
